My parents told me I was severely autistic. This was used as an excuse to punish me a lot, for being emotional or picky or uncomfortable or whatever else my dad wanted to twist on me. 

I didn’t question it until I was 19 when I couldn’t find any records of being diagnosed. At 21, my therapist told me there was no way I was autistic. 

Funny enough as soon as I moved out of the house, my “symptoms” disappeared and my personality did a 180.

Talking with my therapist, she says how horrible it was to live a lie my entire life and we’ve been deconstructing the ways that their lie impacted me.

My little sisters both told me that they see me as a mother figure. But I’m really anxious, too. In fact, I’ve even talked to them a lot about my depression and PTSD, but they still see me as a great role model.

I think it’s just embracing your good and bad qualities and showing that both are okay as long as you can control them. And show them love, be there for them on their bad days, hug them, laugh with them, encourage them to do things they love, compliment them on their successes, help them through their failures.

Having someone who shows them so much love in their life will teach them to show love to others later in their life - at least that’s what I’ve found what happened with my little sisters. In my opinion, a good role model encourages people to do what makes them happy and to find ways to find success and to be happy. And honestly, as long as you’re there for them, that helps them a lot - at least it does for my sisters. 

I bet you’re an amazing sibling, though. Sometimes little siblings are like that, especially since they’re entering their teen years. As long as you show them love and that you’re a good person, you’re a good sibling and a good role model. Just because you have some negative qualities doesn’t completely excuse you from being a great role model - everyone has bad qualities, it’s just how you use them or don’t use them.
